name: Quebec nationalism
summary: Quebec nationalism holds that the French-speaking Québécois form a distinct nation whose language, culture and political autonomy must be protected, using the Quebec state as its main instrument. Since the Quiet Revolution it has been a secular, civic and territorial nationalism that ranges from outright independence (Parti Québécois, Bloc Québécois) to autonomist federalism (CAQ), combining French-language laws, laicity rules and a state role in the economy.
scope: Mainstream contemporary Quebec nationalism since the Quiet Revolution, as embodied by René Lévesque's Parti Québécois, the Charter of the French Language, the laicity law and the autonomist CAQ. It excludes the older clerico-nationalism of Lionel Groulx except as history, and fringe ethnic or extremist groups.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Quiet Revolution made the state the provider of health care and welfare in place of the Church, and mainstream nationalist parties defend that public system.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Nationalist parties favour a state role in building Francophone economic strength, though the CAQ is business-friendly; the mainstream is a mixed economy.

public-ownership.rationale: The Quiet Revolution's hydroelectric nationalisation and state enterprise were meant to give Francophones control of the economy, and that legacy is still defended.

unions-good.rationale: The PQ has traditionally drawn support from organized labour, though ties are informal.

cut-welfare.rationale: The welfare state is a Quiet Revolution achievement and part of the national project, although PQ governments have also cut spending at times.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not an issue the nationalist tradition addresses; adherents are divided across parties.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Nationalist parties are not distinguished by a position here; supporters of Bill 21 and critics both invoke tolerance.

state-harmful.rationale: Nationalism sees the (Quebec) state as the main tool for national emancipation, so the claim that the state is harmful is rejected.

decide-locally.rationale: Quebec nationalists want decisions in Quebec's jurisdictions taken by Quebec and not by Ottawa; Bill 99 s13 and the Séguin report's rejection of the federal spending power say so (s7, s11). The principle applies to the province, and the Act also has the Québec State encouraging local and regional communities to take responsibility for their development (s.10).

traditional-family.rationale: Since the Quiet Revolution secularised society, mainstream nationalism no longer defends Church-based family models, though the older clerical strand did.

more-religion-public.rationale: The mainstream stresses laicity, and Bill 21 bars religious symbols for public officials in authority.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Adherents are split, with attention going to national and Indigenous questions more than racial remedies.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Defending Québécois culture and the French language is the core purpose of the ideology.

gradual-change.rationale: The Quiet Revolution and the sovereignty project sought rapid structural change, but within constitutional and democratic means.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Québec government's 2026-2029 plan lowers permanent admissions to about 45,000 a year and cuts temporary residents by 13 percent against 2024, linking this to the share of French-speaking newcomers (s10); the PQ goes further, and the movement mainly backs lower levels.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Sovereigntists want Quebec to take its own place internationally, but the sources give no view on strengthening the UN.

free-trade.rationale: Sovereignty-association was designed to preserve free trade with Canada; the sources give no general position.

nation-first.rationale: Quebec nationalism puts Quebec's interests first relative to Canada, but is not generally hostile to global cooperation.

open-borders.rationale: The mainstream wants immigration limited to protect French and integration, which rules out open borders.

revolution-justified.rationale: The modern movement pursues independence via referendum and rejects violence; the 1837 rebellion is historical memory, not programme.

central-planning.rationale: Nationalism favours state direction in a market economy rather than a planned one.

socialized-markets.rationale: Cooperative and state firms are accepted but not a doctrine; adherents split.

basic-income.rationale: No nationalist position, as the sources describe the tradition.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Quebec Inc. and the Quiet Revolution used state investment tools to build Francophone-controlled enterprise.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Nationalism operates within a market economy and has no such aim. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Sovereigntists plan their own monetary arrangements, not abolition of central banking.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The tradition is liberal-democratic in structure; clerical corporatism belonged to the older strand.

one-party-rule.rationale: The PQ and other parties compete in elections and referendums.

democracy-best.rationale: Self-determination by referendum is the movement's chosen route, putting democratic legitimacy at its core.

direct-votes.rationale: The movement relies on referendums for sovereignty, but supports representative government for ordinary law.

workers-councils.rationale: No part of the tradition proposes councils replacing parliament.

right-to-secede.rationale: Bill 99 states that the Québec people has an inalienable right to freely decide its political regime and legal status, decides alone how it is exercised, and that a referendum is won with fifty percent plus one (ss.1-4); it was adopted against the federal Clarity Act (s7). The claim is made for Quebec as a nation, and the same Act bars changing Quebec's borders without the National Assembly (s.9).

natural-rulers.rationale: The movement rests on democratic and national-majority legitimacy.

political-violence-never.rationale: The mainstream movement is committed to peaceful referendum; the 1970s FLQ is not its representative.

war-builds-character.rationale: No tradition of militarism; the movement is civic and cultural.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Quiet Revolution separated church and state, and the 2019 law declares Quebec a lay state on separation and neutrality.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Laicity law sets state neutrality, rejecting scriptural law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Nationalism relies on a strong Quebec state.

military-superiority.rationale: Not a nationalist aim; Quebec is not a state with an army.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The dominant model since Lesage is territorial and civic, with a nation defined by shared French-language public culture.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Nationalists see national rather than class conflict as primary, though left-leaning strands exist.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Centre-left parties support redistribution, but not strict equality of outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The first PQ government recognised Indigenous self-determination provided Quebec's territorial integrity was unaffected, so authority over land is only partial.

civilizational-union.rationale: Not a nationalist aim, which focuses on Quebec's own state.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The tradition stresses collective national solidarity.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Quebec nationalists generally defend rights; Bill 21 limits some, but is argued as laicity, not duty.

limit-population.rationale: Demographic strength of French speakers has been a concern, favouring births and integration over limits.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The tradition is modernizing and developmentalist.

restore-past-order.rationale: The mainstream sees the Quiet Revolution as progress; the older clerico-nationalist strand wanted restoration but is marginal today.

direct-action.rationale: The movement prefers elections and referendums.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Nationalism has nothing in common with primitivism. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The tradition supports social programmes but not need-based distribution as an end state.

production-for-use.rationale: It works within a market economy.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not a nationalist claim; left wings of the movement might partly accept it.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Alien to a democratic national movement.

collective-farming.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not a nationalist claim, as the sources describe the tradition.

taxation-theft.rationale: The movement relies on a state financed by taxes, with public finances part of its case for independence.

harm-principle.rationale: Laicity restrictions on public workers go beyond harm, but this is not a general liberal-liberty question for adherents.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Nationalism asserts collective national rights, including self-determination and language rights, alongside individual rights.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Voice and self-government are central, not exit.

state-as-business.rationale: The state is a vehicle of national purpose, not a firm.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Contradicts the civic model of the nation.

organic-representation.rationale: The clerical strand favoured corporatism; mainstream accepts party representation.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Quiet Revolution framed a modernising awakening but not decadence-and-rebirth; adherents divided.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The movement seeks independence within Quebec's existing borders.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

bound-labor.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

single-common-good.rationale: The tradition works through parties and interest competition.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Left-leaning supporters may agree, but it is not a nationalist demand.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Quiet Revolution built public education; vouchers conflict with that tradition.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: PQ governments have both balanced budgets and run deficits; adherents split.

economic-freedom.rationale: The movement links freedom to national self-government rather than markets.

rule-by-example.rationale: Law-based, as the sources describe the tradition.

national-self-determination.rationale: Quebecers form a distinct nation entitled to decide their own political status.

class-collaboration.rationale: The older clerical strand favoured it, the modern left-leaning strand does not.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Heritage and culture preservation is core.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Secular modern nationalism backs gender equality.

ban-interest.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The state is seen as a national instrument.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Bill 84 sets out "national integration" as distinct from Canadian multiculturalism but says newcomers are to enrich Québec culture "without denying their culture of origin", asking for adherence to a French-language common culture rather than assimilation (s9).

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy claim not part of mainstream nationalism, although fringe groups are noted as extremist.

proportional-representation.rationale: Sovereigntists have long backed electoral reform, but the sources do not confirm this.

national-mission.rationale: Aims at self-preservation, not spreading a system.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Quebec nationalism article describes Lesage's Quiet Revolution view that 'the state was the engine to end the relative economic dispossession of French Canadians', an activist state far beyond defence, justice and property.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The civic model upholds equal citizenship; some contested measures like Bill 21 cause critics to dispute it.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Sovereigntists see themselves as a conquered people and a colonized one, but the statement concerns settler states and adherents split on this.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Freedom of conscience is a stated principle of Quebec laicity.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Quiet Revolution secularised schooling, and Quebec removed confessional schooling.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Not applicable to a democratic national movement.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Referendum-based self-determination rests on consent of the governed.

population-transfer.rationale: The civic model and the sources reject exclusion by ethnicity, though Parizeau's remarks caused controversy.

separated-powers.rationale: Bill 99 describes the Québec State as having a government, a National Assembly and impartial, independent courts, so adherents accept divided powers (s7); Bill 21 preamble and override clause (s8) show the movement also favours parliamentary sovereignty over court review, so the check is only weakly held.

vanguard-party.rationale: The PQ is a democratic party competing for votes. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The PQ has ties to labour, as the sources describe the tradition.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Adherents are split between those who see diversity as a challenge for French integration and those who embrace interculturalism.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Lévesque's sovereignty-association proposed a customs and monetary union with common institutions, modelled on the European Community.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Parliamentary tradition, as the sources describe the tradition.

clerical-rule.rationale: Contradicts laicity, as the sources describe the tradition.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The secular modern movement defends cultural expression, unlike the older clerical strand.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Older clerico-nationalism idealised rural life, but the modern mainstream does not.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The state school system is secular.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The territorial model makes belonging a matter of residence and language, not descent.

minority-language-support.rationale: Québec law recognizes the right of First Nations and Inuit to preserve and develop their languages and respects the English-speaking community's long-established institutions (s7, s9), and the movement defends French as a minority language in North America. The Charter of the French Language restricts English in public life, so adherents are mixed on English.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The laicity law denies exemptions from neutrality rules for religious symbols.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Quiet Revolution tied political empowerment to Francophone economic control.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Sovereigntist plans include an elected assembly drafting a Quebec constitution; the Act respecting the future of Quebec is cited.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement is democratic, as the sources describe the tradition.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Quiet Revolution transferred education and welfare from the Church to the state, and the laicity law curbs religious display in public roles.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Sovereigntists treat Quebec's choice as a democratic right and condemn limits like the Clarity Act, so they oppose coercion.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Sovereignty-association and autonomist federalism both seek a Quebec with its own legal and economic powers.

sacred-ruler.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Rule-of-law tradition, as the sources describe the tradition. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Not applicable, as the sources describe the tradition.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The movement's claim is limited to Quebec's territory.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Laicity Act names 'freedom of conscience and freedom of religion' among the four principles on which Quebec's state laicity rests, which rules out punishing anyone for leaving a faith.

women-must-cover.rationale: The face-covering rules require uncovering for public services, the opposite.

common-currency.rationale: Sovereigntists have considered both keeping the Canadian dollar and a Quebec currency.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Francophonie ties exist but no union aim.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The movement is split on the "rather than a state of its own" clause: the PQ and Bloc seek a Quebec state, the CAQ seeks greater autonomy within Canada (s1, s4). Quebecers also form the majority in Quebec, not a minority within it.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Quebec invoked the notwithstanding clause for Bill 21 and Bill 96 to keep courts from overriding the National Assembly's choices.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

moral-incentives.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The mainstream rejects the FLQ method.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The movement sees itself as a colonized people.

delink-world-market.rationale: Sovereignty-association was meant to preserve trade ties. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Quebec has its own charter but resists federal Charter limits on legislative will.

elective-rulers.rationale: Democratic tradition, as the sources describe the tradition.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Patriote tradition invoked such resistance (Ninety-Two Resolutions).

parliament-supreme.rationale: The National Assembly's sovereignty is defended against courts through the notwithstanding clause.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement is political, as the sources describe the tradition. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

native-born-offices.rationale: The territorial civic model includes naturalised citizens, though some proposals tie office to French knowledge.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Not a position; first PQ government accepted self-determination only without affecting territorial integrity.

military-guardian-role.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The Quebec pension plan was a Quiet Revolution public institution.

land-use-tenure.rationale: No strand of Quebec nationalism advocates this; it is foreign to the tradition as the sources describe it.

worker-ownership.rationale: Labour-aligned supporters may like cooperatives, but collective worker ownership is not a nationalist demand and adherents split.

single-official-language.rationale: The Charter of the French Language makes French the language of schooling, signage and business, the movement's signature policy.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: The movement is built on a people's right to self-determination, including leaving a union by referendum, so forced intervention to hold a member in is rejected.

industrial-unions.rationale: Quebec labour movement is close to nationalism, but craft versus industry organisation is not a nationalist issue.

informal-organisation.rationale: The Parti Québécois and Bloc Québécois are permanent parties and the movement is organised through parties and unions, so informal small-group organising is rejected.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Bill 99 s7 makes the Québec State bound by a treaty only with the National Assembly's or Government's formal consent, which leans toward national precedence, but s1 grounds secession in the international principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples, so adherents pull both ways.

religious-nation.rationale: Contemporary Quebec nationalism is secular and the laicity law separates state from religion; the nation is defined by language and culture, not religion.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The Séguin report argued Quebec lacks fiscal resources to match its jurisdictions and rejected the federal spending power (s11), but it asked to reform equalization, not end it, and Quebec is a recipient; sovereigntists want Quebec taxes spent by Quebec while the movement does not reject sharing between provinces.

treaties-binding.rationale: Bill 99 s11 has the Québec State recognize the existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the Aboriginal nations of Québec, and s12 commits it to harmonious relations with them; the statement's "until both parties agree" wording is not tested in the sources.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Quiet Revolution Quebec is secular and liberal on this issue; the PQ and Quebec state have long protected gay rights, and the Charter's era broke with clerical morality.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The movement works through elections and referendums, and the sources show it as a democratic one.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The laicity law enforces state neutrality toward religion and the Quiet Revolution ended the Church's role in the state, so the state punishing blasphemy is the opposite of its stance.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The laicity law makes the state religiously neutral, and the nationalism is secular and democratic, so removing rulers by force for not following religious law contradicts it.

assisted-dying.rationale: Quebec's National Assembly passed the first provincial medical aid in dying law in 2014, with broad cross-party support including PQ members, so the nationalist mainstream backs it.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Act respecting the laicity of the State establishes the state's separation from religion, and Quiet Revolution nationalism replaced clerical authority with popular sovereignty.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Bill 21 bars officials in authority positions and public-school teachers and principals from wearing religious symbols at work, and the nationalist mainstream backs it (s8). The Act does not cover pupils, and some nationalists oppose it, so the statement is only partly matched.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Modern Quebec nationalism is a democratic, civic movement working through elected institutions, with no role for hereditary rule.

property-franchise.rationale: Civic nationalism rests on universal citizenship and democratic sovereignty of the Quebec people.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The movement works through statutes such as the Charter of the French Language and the laicity law, passed openly in the National Assembly under the rule of law.

racial-franchise.rationale: Since the Quiet Revolution the movement is civic and territorial, open to all residents regardless of ancestry.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The laicity law makes the state secular and neutral between religions, which is incompatible with legal restrictions on interfaith marriage.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Civic, secular nationalism opposes targeting religious minorities; the laicity framework is about state neutrality, not private boycotts.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The laicity law keeps the state neutral and secular, not atheistic, and does not promote atheism in schools.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Quiet Revolution moved welfare from the Church to the state, and the mainstream parties defend that public role over charity.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Quiet Revolution era reforms established spousal equality in Quebec's civil law, which mainstream nationalist parties support.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Mainstream Quebec nationalism since the Quiet Revolution is a secular, civic, democratic movement with no tradition of drilled national-service youth movements.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The Quiet Revolution secularised Quebec nationalism and the laicity law keeps the state religiously neutral, so it does not sanctify the national dead; the Patriotes are commemorated in a civic way.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Post-Quiet-Revolution nationalism is secular and framed in terms of language, democracy and interests, and the laicity law separates state and religion.

culture-before-state.rationale: Post-Quiet Revolution nationalism treats the state as the instrument of cultural protection: Bill 84 says the Québec State must continue building the constitutional foundations on which the nation stands, and Bill 99 asserts state powers to defend the nation (s9, s7), not waiting on cultural renewal first.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Bill 99 s9 says Quebec's territory and boundaries cannot be altered without the National Assembly's consent and that territorial integrity must be maintained (s7); Quebec nationalism since the 1960s defines the people by territory and has not sought to merge francophone regions of other provinces into Quebec.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The Quiet Revolution made the state, not the Church or private owners, the provider of health, welfare and hydro power, and nationalist parties defend this.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Post-Quiet-Revolution nationalism is secular and defends laicity rules, so it does not frame politics as serving a spiritual nature.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Bill 99 s13 states that no other parliament or government may reduce the powers, authority, sovereignty or legitimacy of the National Assembly, and the Assembly never adhered to the 1982 Constitution; sovereigntists and autonomists alike reject powers that Ottawa could withdraw (s7).

racial-group-interests.rationale: Mainstream Quebec nationalism is civic and territorial, not racial, and defines the nation by language and culture.

language-defines-nation.rationale: The Québec people is defined as the majority French-speaking people of a territory, and the State draws its legitimacy from "the people inhabiting its territory" (Bill 99 preamble and s.5; Bill 84), so Quebec nationalism since the Quiet Revolution does not take language and history to form one nation across provincial borders, and it includes non-francophone Quebecers.

communal-electorates.rationale: Modern Quebec nationalism is civic and secular and the laicity law keeps religion out of public life, so religiously separate electorates are contrary to it.

free-public-college.rationale: Quebec has the lowest tuition in Canada, a legacy of the Quiet Revolution, and the movement has supported free or near-free education, but it is not a core platform item.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The Quiet Revolution aligned nationalism with a strong union movement and social-democratic policy, as in the Parti Québécois tradition.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Quebec has a balanced-budget law, but nationalist parties differ on fiscal rules; not a stated nationalist position.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Mainstream Quebec nationalism pursues sovereignty by referendum and uses the Quebec state as its main instrument, rejecting smashing it.

sacred-nation.rationale: Post-Quiet-Revolution Quebec nationalism is secular, civic and territorial, so describing the nation as sacred does not fit.

internal-colonialism.rationale: A decolonial strand (Vallières, the FLQ, Parti pris) compared French Canadians to a colonised people, but the mainstream post-1960 parties argue from self-determination and fiscal imbalance (s4, s11) rather than exploitation by a wealthy centre, and Quebec is not a poor periphery in their account.

workers-own-party.rationale: The Parti Québécois is a broad-based national party and the movement holds no unified view on a separate workers' party.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Quebec nationalists define French as a distinct national language but have no stated view on how others name languages.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The Charter of the French Language makes French the common public language, and nationalists favour newcomers learning it and integrating into the French-speaking nation.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Quebec nationalism is closely tied to its strong union movement and the Parti Québécois's labour-friendly platform, which opposes right-to-work rules; Quebec also has the Rand formula.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Nationalists treat democratic self-determination by referendum and election as the legitimate route, and the movement defends its procedures as democratic, though it also pursues policies such as language rules.

premarital-sex.rationale: The Quiet Revolution secularised Quebec society and ended the Church's moral authority, so mainstream nationalists accept sex outside marriage.

negative-income-tax.rationale: The Quebec state-centred model defends public welfare and social programs, so nationalist parties would not replace welfare with a negative income tax.

women-suffrage.rationale: Women's suffrage in Quebec came in 1940, and modern nationalist parties embrace equality of rights as a basic value of Quebec society.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Quebec has a dedicated Secrétariat à la condition féminine and Conseil du statut de la femme, created in the post-Quiet Revolution state-building era, and the nationalist parties defend them.

national-church-status.rationale: The laicity law bars religious privilege in the state, so a national church with a special legal status is rejected.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The movement claims territorial autonomy or sovereignty for French-speaking Quebec, and Bill 99 recognizes the Aboriginal nations' right to autonomy within Québec (preamble); sovereigntists would go beyond autonomy, and Quebec nationalism describes the nation as civic, not ethnic.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: The movement's route to sovereignty is a referendum in which Quebec's inhabitants decide for themselves.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Modern Quebec nationalism is civic and secular, and the sources do not frame the tie to land as spiritual; adherents split.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Taxation of consumption is not a nationalist issue; parties differ.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The laicity law and the Quiet Revolution's break from Church-run politics support cutting politics across, and apart from, religious lines.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Quebec nationalism combines modernity with preserving French culture, but not archaic ancestral values; adherents split.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Quebec nationalism is not organised around a theory of distributive justice, and the movement is centre-left in practice; adherents are not aligned.

multipolar-world.rationale: Quebec nationalism seeks national self-determination within the existing order, not a multipolar world as such; adherents are not aligned.

material-over-identity.rationale: Quebec nationalism puts language and cultural identity at the centre of its politics, ahead of narrowly material demands.

missingStatements.text: A state may require one language to be the common language of schooling, work and commerce, even where this restricts the use of other languages.
missingStatements.rationale: The Charter of the French Language makes French the language of instruction, signage and business, the movement's signature policy.

missingStatements.text: A region's secession should be subject to conditions set by the national parliament, such as a clear question and a clear majority.
missingStatements.rationale: Sovereigntists consider the Clarity Act illegitimate and hold that Quebec alone should set the terms of secession.

missingStatements.text: Public employees in positions of authority should be barred from wearing religious symbols at work.
missingStatements.rationale: The 2019 laicity law bans such symbols for judges, police and teachers, and the nationalist parties support it.

notes: Parties differ: the PQ and Bloc seek independence, the CAQ is autonomist; the older clerical strand and Bill 21's critics within the movement would answer religion and family statements differently. Many answers are low-confidence inferences from the secular, centre-left post-1960 mainstream.
